1: # Contributing
2: 
3: Bug reports, benchmarks on your hardware, fixes and new model support are all
4: welcome. The short version of the rules is in
5: [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Veloresearch/kinetic/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md);
6: this chapter explains how the code fits together and walks through the two
7: most common contributions: a new architecture and a new weight format.
8: 
9: For anything larger than a small fix, open an issue first so we can agree on
10: the approach. The [good first issues](https://github.com/Veloresearch/kinetic/labels/good%20first%20issue)
11: are a good place to start.
12: 
13: ## How the code is laid out
14: 
15: <p align="center">
16: <picture>
17:   <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="diagrams/architecture-dark.svg">
18:   <img src="diagrams/architecture-light.svg" alt="Kinetic in six layers: terminal, server and libraries on top; RAD-1, Warm Start, Zero Wait and Convoy, each switchable with --off; model families Qwen3.5, Gemma, LFM, Llama and a new family, one file each; shared blocks attention, delta-net, mamba2, short-conv and MoE; devices CPU, CUDA and Vulkan; GGUF and .ktc files" width="100%">
19: </picture>
20: </p>
21: 
22: | Crate | Holds |
23: |---|---|
24: | `kinetic-gguf` | the GGUF reader: header, metadata, memory-mapped tensors |
25: | `kinetic-quant` | `TensorType` and the scalar reference dequantization of every format: the definition the fast kernels are tested against |
26: | `kinetic-cpu` | AVX2 kernels: matrix-vector products per format, norms, rotary embeddings, the thread pool |
27: | `kinetic-models` | the shared blocks (`blocks/`), the architectures built from them (`arch/`), the CUDA executor (`cuda/`), speculative decoding (`speculative/`), Warm Start (`warm/`), Shortlist (`head/`) |
28: | `kinetic-cuda` | the CUDA driver API, the kernels (`cuda/*.cuh`) and their launchers |
29: | `kinetic-tokenizer` | BPE, SentencePiece and WordPiece tokenizers read from GGUF metadata |
30: | `kinetic-grammar` | GBNF and JSON Schema to a token mask |
31: | `kinetic-vision` | image encoders (`mmproj` files) |
32: | `kinetic-ktc` | the `.ktc` format: reader, writer, verification |
33: | `kinetic-server` | the engine (chat template, sampling, tool calls) and the HTTP server |
34: | `kinetic-cli` | the `kinetic` command |
35: | `kinetic`, `kinetic-capi` | the Rust and C libraries; `bindings/python` builds on `kinetic` |
36: 
37: ## What every change must keep
38: 
39: - **Exactness.** Anything that speeds up decoding must give the same tokens
40:   as plain decoding. In practice this means a batch of tokens must produce,
41:   bit for bit, the logits those tokens produce one at a time. The identity
42:   tests below check it; a change that breaks them is not mergeable, however
43:   fast.
44: - **Own code.** No code copied from other inference engines. Reading
45:   llama.cpp's sources to understand a format or an architecture is fine and
46:   expected; tables and grids of a format are data, and their source goes
47:   into `NOTICE`.
48: - **No network.** Kinetic never connects to the network, except when you
49:   run `kinetic pull`. Nothing else may open a connection.
50: - **Small files with one job**, doc comments on public items, comments only
51:   where the reason is not obvious, `unsafe` only at FFI, SIMD and kernel
52:   boundaries with a `// SAFETY:` comment.
53: - **Numbers for speed claims**: model, hardware, command, before and after,
54:   best of several runs.
55: 
56: ## Adding an architecture
57: 
58: [Adding a model family](adding-a-family.md) walks through it: a scaffold
59: script, the blocks and what each covers, mapping GGUF tensors, the family
60: descriptor, the conformance check against llama.cpp and the identity gates.
61: 
62: <p align="center">
63: <picture>
64:   <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="diagrams/add-a-family-dark.svg">
65:   <img src="diagrams/add-a-family-light.svg" alt="Five steps from left to right: scaffold from a GGUF, map its tensors to blocks in one file, add one line to the registry, check conformance against llama.cpp, open a pull request" width="100%">
66: </picture>
67: </p>
68: 
69: 
70: ## Adding a weight format or a kernel
71: 
72: Every format is defined once, by its reference dequantization, and every
73: fast kernel is tested against that definition.
74: 
75: 1. **The type.** `crates/kinetic-quant/src/types.rs`: the GGUF type id,
76:    elements and bytes per block, and the name.
77: 2. **The definition.** A block decoder in `crates/kinetic-quant/src/dequant/`,
78:    wired into `dequantize`. Straightforward scalar code; this is what "correct"
79:    means for the format. Lookup grids go in `grids/` with their source noted
80:    in `NOTICE`.
81: 3. **The CPU kernel.** A dot product against 8-bit activations in
82:    `crates/kinetic-cpu/src/kdot/`, with an AVX2 version where it pays.
83:    `kdot/tests.rs` compares every kernel with the reference on random
84:    blocks. Until a kernel exists, `matvec` falls back to dequantizing rows,
85:    so a new format works on the CPU from step 2 on.
86: 4. **The CUDA kernel.** A GEMV in `crates/kinetic-cuda/cuda/`, its entry in
87:    `WEIGHT_TYPES` (`src/gemv.rs`) and its field layout (`src/layout.rs`),
88:    tested in `tests/gemv_quants.rs` against the reference and an f64 dot
89:    product, alone and batched. Expert kernels for mixture-of-experts models
90:    are separate (`src/moe.rs`, `tests/moe.rs`).
91: 5. **The docs.** The format table in [Models and formats](models.md).
92: 
93: Batched kernels must give each row exactly what the single-row kernel gives.
94: That is what keeps speculative decoding and Warm Start exact; the GEMV tests
95: check it.
96: 
97: ## Sign your work
98: 
99: Kinetic uses the [Developer Certificate of Origin](https://developercertificate.org)
100: (DCO) 1.1. By adding a `Signed-off-by` line to a commit you certify that you
101: wrote the change or otherwise have the right to submit it under the
102: project's license:
103: 
104: ```sh
105: git commit -s -m "models: add lfm2"
106: ```
107: 
108: Pull requests with unsigned commits cannot be merged. To sign commits you
109: already made, run `git rebase --signoff main` and force-push your branch.

//! Compiles `cuda/kernels.cu` into one fatbin that `src/kernels.rs` embeds.
//!
//! Without nvcc an empty image is written instead, so the crate still builds
//! and `Kernels::load` reports at runtime that the kernels were not built.
//! A failing nvcc, on the other hand, fails the build.

use std::env;
use std::fs;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
use std::process::Command;

const SOURCE: &str = "cuda/kernels.cu";

/// Machine code for each architecture from Pascal on, plus PTX for
/// compute_90 and compute_120 so the driver can compile for GPUs newer than
/// this list (PTX only runs on devices of at least its compute capability).
///
/// Pascal (sm_60, sm_61) and Volta (sm_70) have no tensor-core instructions
/// that the kernels use; there the kernels that need them are never
/// launched. CUDA 13 no longer builds for them, see [`LAST_CUDA_FOR`].
/// `KINETIC_CUDA_ARCHS` replaces this list, see [`gencodes`].
const GENCODE: &[&str] = &[
    "arch=compute_60,code=sm_60",
    "arch=compute_61,code=sm_61",
    "arch=compute_70,code=sm_70",
    "arch=compute_75,code=sm_75",
    "arch=compute_80,code=sm_80",
    "arch=compute_86,code=sm_86",
    "arch=compute_89,code=sm_89",
    "arch=compute_90,code=[sm_90,compute_90]",
    "arch=compute_120,code=[sm_120,compute_120]",
];

/// The architectures of [`GENCODE`] that a CUDA release after this one no
/// longer builds for.
const LAST_CUDA_FOR: (u32, &[&str]) = (12, &["60", "61", "70"]);

fn main() {
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=cuda");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-env-changed=NVCC");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-env-changed=CUDA_PATH");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-env-changed=KINETIC_CUDA_ARCHS");

    let out = PathBuf::from(env::var_os("OUT_DIR").expect("OUT_DIR is set by cargo"))
        .join("kernels.fatbin");
    let Some(nvcc) = find_nvcc() else {
        println!("cargo:warning=nvcc not found: CUDA kernels not built");
        fs::write(&out, []).expect("write empty kernel image");
        return;
    };

    let mut cmd = Command::new(&nvcc);
    cmd.args(["-fatbin", "-O3", "-std=c++17", "-o"])
        .arg(&out)
        .arg(SOURCE);
    for gencode in gencodes(nvcc_release(&nvcc)) {
        cmd.args(["-gencode", &gencode]);
    }
    // nvcc 12 warns that sm_60 to sm_70 are deprecated; they still build.
    cmd.arg("-Wno-deprecated-gpu-targets");
    if cfg!(windows) {
        // nvcc checks the MSVC version against a list fixed at its release;
        // newer toolsets compile these kernels fine.
        cmd.arg("-allow-unsupported-compiler");
    }
    if let Some(ccbin) = find_msvc() {
        cmd.arg("-ccbin").arg(ccbin);
    }
    let status = cmd
        .status()
        .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("running {}: {e}", nvcc.display()));
    assert!(status.success(), "nvcc failed to compile {SOURCE}");
}

# Models and formats

Kinetic reads GGUF files as llama.cpp and the Hugging Face GGUF tools write
them, and its own `.ktc` files. It does not convert anything: you point it
at a file on your disk.

The quickest check for a file is `kinetic info`:

```sh
kinetic info Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf
```

```text
Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf
  name           Qwen3.5-4B
  architecture   qwen35
  size           2.64 GiB, 4.33 B parameters
  context        262144 tokens
  layers         33, width 2560
  prediction     yes (drafts for speculative decoding)
  weights        Q4_K    149 tensors    1478.0 MiB
                 Q6_K     35 tensors    1018.2 MiB
                 Q5_K     24 tensors     165.0 MiB
                 F32     232 tensors      18.7 MiB
                 Q8_0      1 tensors      13.3 MiB
  tokenizer      gpt2 (qwen35), 248320 tokens, BOS none, EOS <|im_end|>
  chat template  7992 bytes
```

An architecture Kinetic does not know is marked `(not supported yet)`. A
known architecture can still use a feature that is not supported yet, such
as a kind of rotary scaling; `kinetic run` then names it when it loads the
file.

## Architectures

The names are the GGUF `general.architecture` values.

| Architecture | Models | CPU | CUDA |
|---|---|:-:|:-:|
| `qwen35` | Qwen3.5, with its multi-token prediction block | yes | yes |
| `qwen35moe` | Qwen3.5 mixture of experts, such as 35B-A3B | yes | yes, also larger than GPU memory |
| `lfm3` | LFM3 | yes | yes |
| `lfm2` | LFM2 | yes | yes |
| `lfm2moe` | LFM2.5 mixture of experts, such as 8B-A1B (experimental, slower than llama.cpp on CUDA for now) | yes | yes, also larger than GPU memory |
| `llama` | Llama 3, Mistral, SmolLM2 and other models built like Llama | yes | yes |
| `qwen2` | Qwen2.5 | yes | yes |
| `qwen3` | Qwen3 | yes | yes |
| `gemma3` | Gemma 3 | yes | yes |
| `gemma4` | Gemma 4 E2B and E4B; the 26B A4B mixture of experts is not supported yet | yes | yes |
| `ernie4_5` | ERNIE 4.5 | yes | yes |
| `hunyuan-dense` | Hunyuan dense models | yes | yes |
| `exaone4` | EXAONE 4.0 | yes | yes |
| `olmo2` | OLMo 2 | yes | yes |
| `granite` | Granite 3 and 4.0 dense models | yes | yes |
| `granitehybrid` | Granite 4.0 H (Mamba-2 hybrid) | yes | yes |
| `granitemoe` | Granite 3 mixture of experts | yes | yes |
| `falcon-h1` | Falcon-H1 | yes | yes |

With `--device auto`, a model that cannot run on the GPU runs on the CPU and
Kinetic prints why. Through Vulkan (`--device vulkan`), `llama`, `qwen2`,
`qwen3`, `lfm3` and `qwen35` models run today; see [Devices](devices.md#vulkan).

### Embedding and ranking models

`kinetic serve` answers `/v1/embeddings` for these and `/v1/rerank` for
rerankers. They run on the CPU.

| Architecture | Models |
|---|---|
| `bert` | BGE and other BERT-style encoders |
| `nomic-bert` | nomic-embed-text |
| `gemma-embedding` | EmbeddingGemma |
| decoders with a pooling type | Qwen3-Embedding |
| rerankers | Qwen3-Reranker |

A file is served as an embedding model when it is an encoder or its metadata
sets a pooling type (`<arch>.pooling_type`).

### Vision

With `kinetic serve <model> --mmproj <projector>`, chat requests may carry
images. The projector file names its vision tower in `clip.projector_type`
(or `clip.vision.projector_type` when it also holds an audio tower):

| Projector type   | Models                          |
|------------------|---------------------------------|
| `qwen3vl_merger` | Qwen3.5, Ternary Bonsai 2       |
| `gemma4v`        | Gemma 4                         |

When the model runs on a CUDA GPU, images are encoded there too. A prompt with images runs
on the GPU when every layer of the model is there, and on the CPU
otherwise. More projectors are [coming](roadmap.md).

Adding a projector type takes one file in `crates/kinetic-vision/src/`:

1. A struct holding the weights, borrowed from the file through `Loader`.
2. A `load` function that reads the hyperparameters and tensors and returns
   the struct boxed as a `Projector`.
3. `impl Projector`: `n_embd_out`, `prepare` (resize and normalize the way
   the model's processor does) and `encode` (pixels to one row per image
   token, row-major over the token grid).
4. One line in `PROJECTORS` in `lib.rs` mapping the `clip.projector_type`
   string to `load`.

Shared pieces live in `ops.rs` (linear, layer and RMS norms, GELU,
bidirectional attention, patch gathering) and `preprocess.rs` (decoding,
the aspect-keeping resize). Check a new type against llama.cpp's
`llama-mtmd-debug --image rainbow -n <size>` with
`cargo run --release -p kinetic-vision --example encode -- <mmproj> rainbow:<size>`:
the first and last values and the sum of the final embeddings should match
to a few digits. On the text side, an image's rows enter the prompt as
`Input::Image`; models with (time, row, column) rotary positions place them
on the image grid, every other model gives them consecutive positions.

### Tokenizers

The tokenizer is read from the file. Kinetic has byte-level BPE
(`tokenizer.ggml.model` = `gpt2`), SentencePiece (`llama`) and WordPiece
(`bert`). BPE models also name a pre-tokenizer (`tokenizer.ggml.pre`); these
== devices summary ==
# Devices and offload

Kinetic runs on x86-64 and Apple Silicon CPUs, on NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA
and on AMD, Intel and NVIDIA GPUs through Vulkan, on Windows, Linux and
macOS. A model larger than the
GPU can still use it: a dense model splits its layers between the GPU and the
CPU, and a mixture-of-experts model keeps its experts in system memory.

## Choosing the device

`run`, `chat`, `serve` and `bench` take `--device`:

| `--device` | Does |
|---|---|
| `auto` (default) | CUDA, then Vulkan, then the CPU: the first that can run the model |
| `cuda` | the first NVIDIA GPU through CUDA, or fail with the reason |
| `vulkan` | the first GPU through Vulkan, or fail with the reason |
| `cpu` | the CPU only |

`none` is accepted for `cpu`, `cuda0` for `cuda` and `vulkan0` for `vulkan`,
as llama.cpp spells them. `-ngl 0` means `--device cpu`, and any other
`-ngl N` means `--gpu-layers N` (see [Dense models larger than the
GPU](#dense-models-larger-than-the-gpu)).

With `auto`, Kinetic skips a GPU it cannot use with one line that says why:

```text
kinetic: running on the CPU; CUDA is not usable: <reason>; Vulkan is not usable: <reason>
```

The reasons are: no NVIDIA driver, a build without the CUDA kernels, a model
whose weights and caches do not fit in the GPU's free memory, or a model
that uses something the GPU code does not have yet (see the CUDA column in
[Models and formats](models.md)). The start-up line of `kinetic serve` and
the status line of `kinetic run` name the device that is used:

```text
Serving Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1
[4 tokens at 273.9 tok/s; prompt 13 tokens at 1727.7 tok/s on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU]
```

Some work always runs on the CPU, whatever `--device` says: prompts that
carry images, and embedding and reranking models.

## CPU

Any x86-64 CPU runs Kinetic. The fast kernels need AVX2, FMA and F16C, which
Intel CPUs have since Haswell (2013) and AMD CPUs since Excavator and every
Ryzen; Kinetic detects them at runtime. Without them it still runs, on a
much slower path.

On Apple Silicon the kernels use NEON and the SDOT instruction, which every
M-series chip has.

## Apple GPUs

On a Mac, `--device metal` (or `vulkan`, the same device) runs the Vulkan
kernels through Metal itself, with nothing to install. `auto` picks it.

`-t` sets the number of threads; by default Kinetic uses every logical CPU,
except on macOS, where it uses the performance cores: a step that waits for
an efficiency core is slower than one that leaves it idle.
Generation is limited by memory bandwidth, so more threads than physical
cores rarely help, and on some machines fewer threads are faster. Measure
with `kinetic bench model.gguf --device cpu -t N`.

## NVIDIA GPUs

GPUs from the Pascal generation (GTX 10 series, Tesla P100) on are
supported, with kernels for compute capability 6.0, 6.1, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0, 8.6,
8.9, 9.0 and 12.0, and PTX that newer drivers compile for later GPUs.

Pascal and Volta (compute capability 6.x and 7.0) have none of the tensor
cores the prompt kernels use. Prompts run there in batches of up to 512
tokens through f32 matrix products of the quantized weights and f32
attention in tiles of 64 queries, with the delta rule (and attention to
heads of 64) taken 16 tokens at a time, so prompts take longer than on
Turing and newer; generation runs the same kernels as on newer GPUs. On the
Tesla P100 and V100 (6.0 and 7.0), whose f16 arithmetic runs at twice the
f32 rate, the products multiply weights and inputs in pairs of f16 values
and apply the scales in f32, about 1.5 times as fast; their results differ
from the f32 products in the last bits, as a different order of summation
would. The Tesla P100 (6.0) also lacks the int8 dot product instruction,
which its kernels do in plain integer arithmetic, with the same results and
less speed. The release binaries and `Dockerfile.cuda` build with CUDA 12
and have kernels for them; a build from source with CUDA 13 does not, see
[Building](building.md).

Kinetic opens the driver library at runtime (`nvcuda.dll` on Windows,
`libcuda.so.1` on Linux) and links nothing from the CUDA toolkit, so:

- you need the NVIDIA driver, not the CUDA toolkit;
- the `cuda` build starts on machines without a GPU and runs on the CPU.

Use a recent driver; the kernels are built with CUDA 12.8, and `nvidia-smi`
shows the highest CUDA version your driver supports in its header. The first
GPU is used unless `--gpus` names others; see [Several GPUs](#several-gpus).

## Vulkan

`--device vulkan` runs models on any GPU with a Vulkan driver: AMD, Intel and
NVIDIA. Today it runs `llama`, `qwen2`, `qwen3`, `lfm3` and `qwen35` models,
with drafting and Warm Start; MoE models and the other architectures are
[coming](roadmap.md). Under `auto`, Vulkan is tried after CUDA, so an NVIDIA
GPU uses CUDA and an AMD or Intel GPU uses Vulkan.

The Vulkan kernels need subgroups of 32. NVIDIA, Intel and AMD's RDNA GPUs
have them; AMD's older GCN and Vega GPUs, among them the integrated graphics
of many Ryzen APUs, only run subgroups of 64, which no driver changes, so
models run on the CPU there and `kinetic doctor` says so.

## Dense models larger than the GPU

When a dense model does not fit in GPU memory, Kinetic puts as many of its
last layers on the GPU as fit, with the cache, and runs the first layers on
the CPU, exactly as the CPU path runs them. Only one hidden state per token
crosses between the two. The status line says how the model was split:

```text
[... on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, 24 of 33 layers, the rest on the CPU]
```

`--gpu-layers N` puts at most `N` layers on the GPU, as llama.cpp's `-ngl N`
does; use it to leave GPU memory for other programs. This works through
CUDA; on Vulkan a model runs wholly on the GPU or on the CPU.

## Several GPUs

`--gpus 0,1` spreads a dense model's layers over CUDA GPUs 0 and 1 (in CUDA's
order, which `kinetic doctor` lists): the first GPU holds the embeddings, the

## Project diagnosis

**What it is**: Kinetic, a Rust inference engine for GGUF models, CPU + CUDA + Vulkan (+ Metal via Vulkan crate), OpenAI-compatible server, CLI, C/Python bindings. ~80k Rust LOC, 39 WGSL shaders, ~30 CUDA headers, 14 crates. Beta 0.1.

**Architecture**:
- Layered: gguf reader → quant reference → CPU kernels → models (arch/blocks) → backend executors (cuda/vulkan) → speculative/warm/shortlist/convoy → server/engine → CLI/bindings.
- `Family` registry, one file per arch, shared blocks. Good extensibility for architectures.
- `Backend` trait at server level: coarse, one `generate` call per request, one backend per concurrent request. Concurrency is multiple model states sharing weights (Convoy) rather than continuous batching inside one executor.
- `Target` trait for speculative decoding: clean seam, exactness invariant.
- Backend-specific executors in `kinetic-models/src/{cuda,vulkan}` duplicate orchestration; `kinetic-cuda` and `kinetic-vulkan` hold drivers/kernels. ~4.5k LOC CUDA executor vs 2.2k LOC Vulkan executor. The Vulkan one records graphs and replays; but `Commands::submit` waits synchronously, one frame at a time.
- Vulkan shaders are WGSL compiled by naga to SPIR-V at build; Metal path reuses WGSL via naga MSL. No cooperative matrix yet. GEMV per format, gemv_many for prompt (32 tokens in flight), no tiled GEMM. That's exactly the 4.4x prefill gap.
- CPU: AVX2 + NEON; no AVX-512/VNNI despite Zen 4 host.
- CUDA: fatbin for sm_60..sm_120, tensor core MMA, flash attention, MoE, graphs — more mature. No BF16/NVFP4/FP8.
- Server: thread-per-connection, fixed max connections; `Connection: close`; no keep-alive, no TLS, no chunked? Let me check. It streams SSE. 45% route coverage.
- Tests: ~500 unit tests; exactness gates (f64 reference, batch invariance, prompt-pass equality). CI: fmt/clippy/tests on 3 OS, C example, Python bindings; no GPU CI, no perf regression CI.
- 0 TODOs is notable discipline.

**Measured state (from PLAN, Nov 22 2026)**:
- Dense 27B IQ3_XXS on RX 9070 XT Vulkan: pp512 261.9 vs llama 1154.2 (4.4x behind); tg128 38.4 vs 40.1 (95%).
- MoE 30B A3B IQ3_XXS: pp512 489 vs 2637 (5.4x); tg128 55.7 vs 181.9 (3.3x). Decode limited by experts read from host memory.
- Qwen3.5 35B A3B Q4_K_M: 31/41 layers, tg 25-27 vs llama 39-40; prompt 86-89 vs 82 (ahead).
- CPU fallback 8.4 t/s on 30B.
- Gaps: HIP backend absent; KV quantized absent; async submission absent; persistent pipeline cache absent; MoE grouped GEMM absent; AVX-512 absent; multi-GPU absent.
- Coverage: 21/180 architectures, 13/68 pretokenizers, ~15/45 routes, 5 quant targets, 2/73 multimodal projectors, 10/~200 C functions.

**Implications for experts**:
The dominant bottleneck is GPU kernel engineering on Vulkan/RDNA4 (prefill GEMM, MoE grouped GEMM/GEMV, async submission, coopmat, KV quant). Second is runtime/scheduler architecture (continuous batching, KV management, memory placement, multi-GPU, graph capture). Third is model coverage (architectures, tokenizers) — high volume but lower architectural risk. Fourth is API/server parity and bindings. Fifth is measurement/CI infrastructure to keep gains honest.

/// Time a client has to send its whole request.
const READ_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30);
/// Time one write may block on a client that stopped reading.
const WRITE_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60);
/// Connections served at once, including those waiting for the model.
const MAX_CONNECTIONS: usize = 64;

/// How the server answers, beyond the model it serves.
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Default)]
pub struct Options {
    /// Every route but `/health` needs `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.
    pub api_key: Option<String>,
}

/// Serves the OpenAI-compatible API, llama-server's and Ollama's on
/// `listener` until the process ends. Requests are handled concurrently; as
/// many as the engine has backends run at once and the rest wait their turn.
pub fn serve(engine: &Engine, listener: TcpListener) {
    serve_with(engine, listener, &Options::default());
}

/// [`serve`] with `options`.
pub fn serve_with(engine: &Engine, listener: TcpListener, options: &Options) {
    let serving = AtomicBool::new(true);
    std::thread::scope(|scope| {
        scope.spawn(|| engine.settle_while_idle(|| serving.load(Ordering::Acquire)));
        serve_routes(listener, options, &|head, body, out| {
            route(engine, head, body, out)
        });
        serving.store(false, Ordering::Release);
        engine.wake();
    });
}

/// Serves `/v1/embeddings` for an embedding model, or `/v1/rerank` for a
/// ranking one, as [`serve`] does.
pub fn serve_embeddings(model: &Embeddings, listener: TcpListener) {
    serve_embeddings_with(model, listener, &Options::default());
}

/// [`serve_embeddings`] with `options`.
pub fn serve_embeddings_with(model: &Embeddings, listener: TcpListener, options: &Options) {
    serve_routes(listener, options, &|head, body, out| {
        embeddings::route(model, head, body, out)
    });
}

type Routes<'r> = dyn Fn(&Head, &[u8], &mut &TcpStream) -> Result<(), ApiError> + Sync + 'r;

fn serve_routes(listener: TcpListener, options: &Options, routes: &Routes) {
    let active = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    std::thread::scope(|scope| {
        for stream in listener.incoming() {
            let Ok(stream) = stream else { continue };
            if stream.set_write_timeout(Some(WRITE_TIMEOUT)).is_err() {
                continue;
            }
            if active.fetch_add(1, Ordering::AcqRel) >= MAX_CONNECTIONS {
                active.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::AcqRel);
                let busy = ApiError {
                    status: 503,
                    message: "the server is busy".into(),
                };
                let _ = send_error(&mut &stream, &busy);
                continue;
            }
            let active = &active;
            scope.spawn(move || {
                let _ = catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(|| handle(options, routes, &stream)));
                active.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::AcqRel);
            });
        }
    });
}

/// Reads from a stream with one deadline for the whole request.
struct Deadline<'s> {
    stream: &'s TcpStream,
    until: Instant,
}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""kinetic against llama.cpp, GPU, recorded the same way every time.

Runs `kinetic bench` and `llama-bench` on the same file in the same session,
for prompt sizes 512 and 2048 and 128 generated tokens, and appends one CSV
row per model and run to `--csv` (default `bench-results.csv`). The commit
of this tree is recorded with the numbers, so a later comparison never mixes
two revisions or two GPU states.

    python scripts/bench_protocol.py MODEL [MODEL ...] --llama-bin path/to/llama-bench
"""

import argparse
import datetime
import json
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PROMPTS = (512, 2048)
GENERATE = 128


def run(cmd):
    return subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)


def kinetic(binary, model, prompt, repetitions):
    out = run(
        [
            binary,
            "bench",
            model,
            "--json",
            "--prompt",
            str(prompt),
            "-r",
            str(repetitions),
        ]

"""Greedy token agreement between Kinetic and llama.cpp on one GGUF file.

the generated tokens one by one. Where they part, it prints llama.cpp's
two likeliest tokens there; a gap under --tie nats is flagged as a
near-tie, which quantized kernels may break either way. Kinetic's tokens
come from a second run with logprobs, whose text has to match the plain
run's.

    python scripts/conformance.py model.gguf --kinetic target/release/kinetic \\
        --llama path/to/llama.cpp/bin --device cpu

def status_of(s):
    head = b""
    while len(head.split(b" ")) < 3:
        chunk = s.recv(64)
        if not chunk:
            break
        head += chunk

fn route(engine: &Engine, head: &Head, body: &[u8], out: &mut impl Write) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
    if ollama::handles(&head.path) {
        ollama::route(engine, head, body, out);
        return Ok(());
    }
    if let Some(answer) = llama::route(engine, head, body, out) {
        return answer;
    }
    match head.path.strip_prefix("/v1").unwrap_or(&head.path) {
        "/health" => {
            expect(head, "GET")?;
            let (slots, busy) = engine.slots();
            send_json(
                out,
                &json!({"status": "ok", "slots_idle": slots - busy, "slots_processing": busy}),
            )
        }
        "/metrics" => {
            expect(head, "GET")?;
            let text = engine.metrics();
            let _ = http::write_response(
                out,
                200,
                "text/plain; version=0.0.4; charset=utf-8",
                text.as_bytes(),
            );
            Ok(())
        }
        "/models" => {
            expect(head, "GET")?;
            send_json(out, &models(engine.name(), engine.context_length()))
        }
        "/chat/completions" => {
            expect(head, "POST")?;
            chat(engine, parse(head, body)?, out)
        }
        "/completions" => {
            expect(head, "POST")?;
            completion(engine, parse(head, body)?, out)
        }
        "/prefill" => {
            expect(head, "POST")?;
            prefill(engine, parse(head, body)?, out)
        }
        "/embeddings" | "/rerank" | "/reranking" => Err(ApiError::invalid(format!(
            "{} generates text; serve an embedding or ranking model for {}",
            engine.name(),
            head.path
        ))),
        _ => Err(not_found(head)),
    }
}

pub(crate) fn expect(head: &Head, method: &str) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
    if head.method == method {
        Ok(())
    } else {
        Err(ApiError {
            status: 405,
            message: format!("use {method} for {}", head.path),
        })

Then **team composition**:

**Cellule minimale (4 personnes) pour attaquer le mur de perf**:
1. AMD GPU kernel engineer (Vulkan first, HIP next)
2. Inference runtime architect
3. Rust systems architect (part-time or same as #2)
4. Performance/QA automation engineer
Plus 1 quantization/numerics advisor (part-time) to guard exactness.

**Équipe complète (8-10)**:
- 2 GPU kernel engineers (Vulkan/RDNA + HIP/ROCm; CUDA/Metal as shared)
- 1 runtime architect
- 1 Rust systems architect
- 1 quantization/numerics
- 1 model integration
- 1 tokenizer/compat
- 1 server/API
- 1 perf/QA
- 1 build/release/bindings
- multimodal as needed.

**Sequencing**:
- Phase 0 (2-4 weeks): baseline + ceilings + GPU CI; no code changes. Perf engineer + GPU engineer.
- Phase 1 (6-10 weeks): Vulkan prompt GEMM + coopmat + async + pipeline cache; runtime scheduler design; exactness gates. Target pp512 ≥ 2x, no tg regression.
- Phase 2 (8-12 weeks): HIP skeleton + GEMV + attention; MoE grouped GEMM; KV q8; AVX-512. Target MoE decode, prefill.
- Phase 3: architecture coverage (MLA/DSA/SSM), tokenizers, server routes; parallel track.
- Phase 4: multimodal, bindings, multi-GPU.

**RACI matrix** (workstreams × roles):
- Vulkan GEMM/coopmat: GPU AMD lead, numerics support, QA.
- MoE: GPU AMD + runtime (placement) + numerics.
- HIP: GPU AMD/HIP.
- Scheduler/KV: runtime lead, Rust architect, QA.
- Quantization: numerics lead, GPU/CPU kernel support.
- Architectures: model integration lead, numerics/QA.
- Tokenizers: tokenizer lead, server for templates.
- Server API: server lead, QA.
- CI/perf: QA lead, build/release.
- Bindings: build/release, server/API.

**How to evaluate**:
- Practical exercise, not LeetCode.
- GPU: given `gemv_many.wgsl` and a matrix, implement a tiled GEMM for Q4_K with split-K; measure on RX 9070 XT; must beat existing by ≥1.5x and pass bit-exact; explain roofline and RGP counters.
- Runtime: propose a scheduler change to support 8 concurrent requests with paged KV and chunked prefill; identify exactness/rollback implications; implement a small prototype or design doc with failure modes.
- Rust: refactor one duplicated CUDA/Vulkan path behind a trait without changing behavior; run tests; explain Send/Sync and unsafe.
- Quant: implement a new block format from reference to kernel; tests; measure.
- Model: add a family from a GGUF; match llama tokens.
- QA: design an experiment that detects a 5% regression with ±8% noise; compute sample size; define controls.
- Red flags: only framework-level (PyTorch), only CUDA, no numerics, "rewrite from scratch", benchmarks without controls, no interest in exactness, can't read a profiler.

**Key insight / recommendation**:
- Don't hire a generic "ML engineer" or "LLM expert"; the bottleneck is GPU systems + runtime + numerics.
- The rarest and most valuable profile is the **AMD GPU compute engineer who understands quantization and exactness** — that's the P0.2/P0.3 path.
- The second rarest is the **inference runtime architect** who can evolve the current `Backend`/Convoy model into a token-level scheduler without breaking RAD-1/Warm Start.
- The third is the **numerics gatekeeper**; without them, speed work will silently break the "same answer" promise, which is the product's differentiator.

//! The generation loop every backend shares: prefill a cached sequence,
//! then decode speculatively under a [`Policy`].

use kinetic_models::speculative::{Decoder, Drafter, Greedy, Policy, Sampler, Target};

use crate::backend::{Job, Timings};
use crate::constrained::Constrained;

/// Prompt tokens per forward pass on the CPU; bounds the activations of
/// long prompts. Prompts are cut at multiples of a backend's chunk, which is
/// also where its warm starts resume, so both run the same batches.
pub const PREFILL_CHUNK: usize = 256;

/// CPU prompt runs give the same bits wherever they are cut on multiples of
/// this many tokens after where they started: delta-net layers run batches
/// of 32 or more in chunks of 16, and fewer token by token.
pub const PREFILL_GRID: usize = 32;

/// A sequence a backend keeps between requests.
pub struct Sequence<S> {
    pub state: S,
    /// Every token `state` has run.
    pub tokens: Vec<u32>,
}

impl<S> Sequence<S> {
    /// Whether `prompt` continues this sequence with at least one new token.
    pub fn continues(&self, prompt: &[u32]) -> bool {
        prompt.len() > self.tokens.len() && prompt.starts_with(&self.tokens)
    }
}

/// A backend that runs a request under any policy; [`generate`] picks the
/// policy the request asks for.
pub trait Run<M: Target> {
    fn run<P: Policy<M>>(
        &mut self,
        prompt: &[u32],
        job: &Job,
        policy: &mut P,
        emit: &mut dyn FnMut(&[u32]) -> bool,
    ) -> Timings;
}

/// Runs `job` on `backend` with greedy choice, seeded sampling or a
/// grammar, as the job asks.
pub fn generate<M: Target, B: Run<M>>(
    backend: &mut B,
    prompt: &[u32],
    job: &Job,
    emit: &mut dyn FnMut(&[u32]) -> bool,
) -> Timings {
    assert!(!prompt.is_empty(), "empty prompt");
    let greedy = job.sampling.is_greedy() && job.logprobs.is_none();
    let sampler = || {
        let sampler = Sampler::new(job.sampling.clone());
        match job.logprobs {
            Some(log) => sampler.with_logprobs(log.clone()),
            None => sampler,
        }
    };
    if let Some((grammar, vocab)) = job.grammar {
        let mut policy = Constrained::new(grammar, vocab, prompt.len(), (!greedy).then(sampler));
        return backend.run(prompt, job, &mut policy, emit);
    }
    if greedy {
        backend.run(prompt, job, &mut Greedy, emit)
    } else {
        backend.run(prompt, job, &mut sampler(), emit)
    }
}

/// Runs the tokens of `prompt` that `seq` has not run in chunks of `chunk`,
/// the leading ones without choosing and the last through `policy`, which
/// chooses the token after the prompt.

Let's refine the diagnostic with precise evidence:

- **Prefill**: `PROMPT_BATCH=128`, `gemv_many.wgsl` keeps weight decode in flight for 32 tokens, no shared-memory tiling/split-K. 4.4x gap. This is the #1 performance target.
- **MoE**: `moe_gemv.wgsl` reads experts one slot at a time; no grouped GEMM; decode limited by host expert reads (PLAN G6: `--gpu-layers` plateau, decode independent of layers). 3.3x decode gap, 5.4x prefill.
- **Async**: `Device::execute` creates a fence, submits, waits (`vkWaitForFences`), frees command buffer. One frame in flight. No timeline semaphores. 5-15% expected, plus graph replay.
- **Pipeline cache**: `create_compute_pipelines(vk::PipelineCache::null(), ...)`; startup cost.
- **KV**: `KvCache` f16 (`DeviceBuffer<u32>` storing f16 bits), contiguous `positions`; no q8/q4; limits context/concurrency.
- **Concurrency**: `Engine.free: Mutex<Vec<(usize, Box<dyn Backend>)>>`; one request per backend; `PREFILL_CHUNK=256`; `MAX_CONNECTIONS=64`; `Connection: close`; no keep-alive/TLS.
- **Duplication**: `kinetic-models/src/cuda` 4.5k LOC vs `vulkan` 2.2k; `kinetic-cuda` 8.5k vs `kinetic-vulkan` 5.9k; adding HIP will multiply.
- **CPU**: AVX2/NEON only; Zen 4 AVX-512 not used; `kdot` dispatch has avx2/neon/scalar; no avx512.
- **Quantization**: 5 targets; no imatrix/IQ encode; no NVFP4/FP8 runtime; BF16 CUDA missing; Vulkan 9 types.
- **Coverage**: 21/180 arch; 13/68 pretokenizers; ~15/45 routes; 2/73 projectors; 10/200 C functions.
- **Measurement**: ~517 tests; CI 3 OS; no GPU CI; scripts exist (`bench_protocol.py`, `bench_vs_llamacpp.py`, `conformance.py`, `server_abuse.py`, `same_answer_demo.py`); PLAN.md is manual; no THEORY.md/ledger yet.
- **Strengths**: 0 TODO/FIXME; doc comments; exactness gates; `Family` registry; `Target` trait; `Backend` trait; `Projector` registry; `.ktc` signed; RAD-1 etc.

Now, detailed P0 profiles.

#### 1. GPU AMD

**Mission**: "Faire passer le préfill Vulkan de 23% à ≥50% de llama.cpp, puis porter les noyaux sur HIP."

**Compétences**:
- Vulkan compute 1.3 (descriptors, push constants, specialization constants, subgroups 32/64, barriers, command buffers, timeline semaphores, pipeline cache, cooperative matrix).
- WGSL/SPIR-V/naga; RGP; AMDGPU ISA; RDNA4 (wave32, LDS, VGPR/SGPR, occupancy, Infinity Cache).
- GEMM tuilé: shared-memory tiling, register blocking, split-K, swizzling, bank conflicts, epilogue.
- Quantization: Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K/Q8_0/IQ3_XXS/IQ4_XS, block scales, dequant-in-registers, packed int8 dot (`v_dot4_i32_i8`, `sdot4`).
- Roofline: measure bandwidth/FLOPS, identify memory vs compute bound.
- Exactness: f32 accumulation, batch invariance, prompt-pass equality.
- Rust/ash/unsafe.

**Pourquoi**:
- `gemv_many.wgsl` = 32 tokens in flight, not a tiled GEMM; `PROMPT_BATCH=128`; no coopmat; 4.4x gap.
- `Commands::submit` waits on a fence; no timeline semaphores; no pipeline cache; 5-15% + startup.
- `moe_gemv.wgsl` reads one expert slot at a time; no grouped GEMM; 3.3x decode / 5.4x prefill.
- `KvCache` f16 only; q8_0 would double context.
- This is the only measured performance gap on the local machine.

**Livrables**:
- Baseline + roofline + RGP profile.
- Tiled Q4_K/IQ GEMM, bit-exact, ≥1.5x.
- Coopmat + split-K, ≥2x; async submission; pipeline cache.
- Grouped MoE GEMM; KV q8_0.
- HIP port of the same kernels.

**KPI**: pp512/pp2048 vs llama Vulkan, tg128 no regression, bit-exact gates, achieved GB/s/TFLOPS, startup.

#### 2. Runtime architect

**Mission**: "Faire passer le serveur de N backends indépendants à un ordonnanceur token-level qui tient cN, TTFT et p99, sans casser RAD-1/Warm Start/Convoy."

**Compétences**:
- Continuous batching, paged KV, prefix caching, chunked prefill, admission control, fairness, priority, cancellation, backpressure.
- Speculative decoding scheduling: draft/verify overlap, tree verification, rollback, KV reuse.
- Rust concurrency: threads/async, Mutex/Condvar, channels, atomics, Send/Sync, scoped threads, panic safety.
- Memory: KV pool sizing, fragmentation/defrag, unified memory, pinned host, MoE expert paging, OOM watchdog.
- Graph capture/replay, multi-stream, overlap.
- Observability: TTFT, tok/s, p50/p99, cache hit, queue depth.

**Pourquoi**:
- `Engine` = `Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn Backend>>>`, one request per backend; `PREFILL_CHUNK=256`; no global scheduler.
- `Convoy` shares passes but doesn't schedule across requests.
- KV contiguous per sequence, no paging; `MAX_CONNECTIONS=64`; `Connection: close`.
- cN/TTFT is the next scalability ceiling after prefill.

**Livrables**:
- Design doc + prototype of token-level scheduler.
- KV pool N×context; chunked prefill; cancellation; per-token metrics.
- c4/c16/c64 benchmarks; p99 and TTFT targets.
- Preserve exactness and Warm Start semantics.

**KPI**: aggregate throughput, p99, TTFT, cache hit, no exactness regression.

#### 3. Rust systems/backend architect

**Mission**: "Réduire la duplication CUDA/Vulkan et préparer HIP/Metal/SYCL sans multiplier les exécuteurs."

**Compétences**:
- Rust avancé: lifetimes, traits, generics vs dyn, zero-copy, unsafe soundness, Send/Sync, Arc/Rc, mmap, allocators, cache-friendly layouts, monomorphization.

# Kinetic — quels experts pour améliorer l’architecture et la performance

## Réponse courte

Le projet n’a pas besoin d’un « expert LLM » générique. Il a besoin de **quatre profils rares sur le chemin critique**, puis de profils de couverture :

1. **Ingénieur noyaux GPU AMD (Vulkan/RDNA 4, puis HIP/ROCm)** — le seul écart de performance mesuré sur la machine locale est là.
2. **Architecte runtime d’inférence** — ordonnancement, KV cache, concurrence, TTFT, p99.
3. **Ingénieur quantification et exactitude numérique** — le garde-fou du différenciateur « même réponse, plus vite ».
4. **Ingénieur performance/qualification** — rendre les gains mesurables, reproductibles et non régressifs.

Autour : **intégration des architectures**, **tokenizers/templates**, **serveur/API**. Le multimodal et les bindings viennent après.

---

## 1. Ce que le dépôt montre

Kinetic est un moteur d’inférence Rust pour fichiers GGUF : CPU, CUDA, Vulkan, Metal via Vulkan, serveur OpenAI-compatible, CLI et bindings. Le dépôt fait environ **81 k lignes de Rust**, **14 crates**, **39 shaders WGSL**, une trentaine d’en-têtes CUDA et **~517 tests**.

**Points forts à préserver :**

- Architecture en couches claire : `kinetic-gguf` → `kinetic-quant` → `kinetic-cpu` → `kinetic-models` (`arch/`, `blocks/`) → exécuteurs CUDA/Vulkan → `kinetic-server` → CLI/bindings.
- Registre `Family` : une architecture = un fichier + une ligne, pas un `match` central.
- Contrat `Target` pour le spéculatif : RAD-1, rollback, arbre de vérification, exactitude.
- Culture de l’exactitude : référence f64, batch-invariance, égalité passe mono-token / passe prompt, tests de non-régression.
- Différenciateurs réels : RAD-1, Warm Start, Zero Wait, Shortlist, Convoy, Flywheel, `.ktc` signé.
- Discipline : zéro `TODO/FIXME`, doc comments, CI Linux/Windows/macOS, `clippy -D warnings`.

**Faiblesses structurelles :**

| Sujet | Constat |
|---|---|
| Duplication backend | `kinetic-models/src/cuda` ≈ 4,5 k LOC vs `vulkan` ≈ 2,2 k LOC ; `kinetic-cuda` ≈ 8,5 k LOC vs `kinetic-vulkan` ≈ 5,9 k LOC. Ajouter HIP/Metal/SYCL va multiplier la maintenance. |
| Runtime | `Engine` = `Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn Backend>>>`, **une requête par backend**. `Convoy` mutualise des passes, mais il n’y a pas d’ordonnanceur token-level avec KV paginé. |
| Vulkan | Soumission **synchrone** (`vkWaitForFences`), pas de timeline semaphores, pas de `VkPipelineCache` persisté, pas de cooperative matrix, KV f16 seulement. |
| Préfill | `gemv_many.wgsl` garde 32 tokens en vol, ce n’est pas un GEMM tuilé : **4,4×** derrière llama.cpp sur un dense 27B. |
| MoE | GEMV groupé lit les experts un slot à la fois ; décodage limité par les lectures d’experts en mémoire hôte : **3,3×** derrière en décodage, **5,4×** en préfill. |
| Couverture | 21/180 architectures, 13/68 prétokenizers, ~15/45 routes serveur, 5 cibles de quantification, 2/73 projecteurs multimodaux. |
| Mesure | Protocole excellent dans `PLAN.md`, mais **manuel** : pas de CI GPU, pas de `THEORY.md`, pas de `ledger.jsonl` automatisé. |

**Chiffres qui dictent les priorités (22 nov. 2026) :**

| Cas | Kinetic Vulkan | llama.cpp Vulkan | Écart |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Dense 27B IQ3_XXS, pp512 | 261,9 t/s | 1154,2 t/s | **4,4×** |
| Dense 27B IQ3_XXS, tg128 | 38,4 t/s | 40,1 t/s | 1,04× |
| MoE 30B A3B, pp512 | 489 t/s | 2637 t/s | **5,4×** |
| MoE 30B A3B, tg128 | 55,7 t/s | 181,9 t/s | **3,3×** |
| Qwen3.5 35B A3B, tg | 25–27 t/s | 39–40 t/s | ~1,5× |

Conclusion : **le décodage dense est déjà à 95 % de llama.cpp**. Le gisement principal est le **préfill GEMM**, le **MoE**, l’**asynchrone**, le **KV quantifié** et l’**ordonnancement**. Ce n’est pas un problème de « modèle » ou de « framework ML » : c’est un problème de **systèmes GPU et de runtime**.

---

### P0 — 1. Ingénieur noyaux GPU AMD (Vulkan/RDNA 4, puis HIP/ROCm)

**Mission :** faire passer le préfill Vulkan de 23 % à ≥ 50 % de llama.cpp, puis porter les mêmes noyaux sur HIP.

**Compétences indispensables :**

- **Vulkan compute 1.3** : descriptors, push constants, specialization constants, subgroups 32/64, barriers, command buffers, timeline semaphores, `VkPipelineCache`, `VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix`.
- **WGSL / SPIR-V / naga**, et si possible GLSL/HLSL. Profilage **RGP** (Radeon GPU Profiler), ISA AMDGPU.
- **Microarchitecture RDNA 4** : wave32, LDS 64 Kio, pression VGPR/SGPR, occupancy, hiérarchie de cache, Infinity Cache.
- **GEMM tuilé** : tuiles en mémoire partagée, register blocking, split-K, swizzling, bank conflicts, épilogue fusionné, FP16/BF16/INT8 dot.
- **Quantification** : Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, Q8_0, IQ3_XXS, IQ4_XS, échelles de blocs, dequant-in-registers, dot int8 packé (`v_dot4_i32_i8`, `sdot4`).
- **Roofline** : mesurer la bande passante et les FLOPS réels, distinguer memory-bound et compute-bound avec des compteurs.
- **Exactitude** : accumulation f32, batch-invariance, égalité passe prompt / passe mono-token. Comprendre `Target` et RAD-1.
- **Rust/ash/unsafe** aux frontières des noyaux.

**Pourquoi ce profil ici :**

- `gemv_many.wgsl` n’est pas un GEMM tuilé ; `PROMPT_BATCH = 128`, 32 tokens en vol, pas de tuile partagée ni de split-K.
- `Commands::submit` soumet puis attend le fence ; pas de timeline semaphores.
- `create_compute_pipelines(vk::PipelineCache::null(), …)` : pas de cache de pipelines persisté.
- `KvCache` est en f16, non quantifié.
- `moe_gemv.wgsl` lit les experts un slot à la fois ; pas de GEMM groupé.
- C’est le **seul écart de performance mesuré** sur la RX 9070 XT.

**Livrables 90 jours :**

1. Baseline reproductible, roofline, profil RGP de pp512.
2. GEMM tuilé Q4_K/IQ, bit-exact, ≥ 1,5×.
3. Coopmat + split-K, ≥ 2× ; soumission asynchrone ; cache de pipelines.
4. GEMM MoE groupé ; KV q8_0.
5. Portage HIP des mêmes noyaux.

**KPI :** pp512/pp2048 vs llama Vulkan, tg128 sans régression, gates bit-exact, GB/s et TFLOPS atteints, temps de démarrage.

---

### P0 — 2. Architecte runtime d’inférence

**Mission :** faire passer le serveur de « N backends indépendants » à un ordonnanceur token-level qui tient la concurrence, le TTFT et le p99, sans casser RAD-1, Warm Start ni Convoy.

**Compétences indispensables :**

- **Continuous batching**, **paged KV**, prefix caching, chunked prefill, admission control, fairness, priorité, annulation, backpressure.
- **Décodage spéculatif** : ordonnancement draft/verify, vérification d’arbre, rollback, réutilisation de KV.
- **Concurrence Rust** : threads/async, `Mutex`/`Condvar`, channels, atomics, `Send`/`Sync`, scoped threads, panic safety.
- **Mémoire** : dimensionnement du pool KV (N × contexte), fragmentation/défrag, mémoire unifiée, pinned host, paging des experts MoE, watchdog OOM.
- **Graph capture/replay**, multi-stream, recouvrement copies/calcul.
- **Observabilité** : TTFT, tok/s, p50/p99, cache hit, profondeur de file.

**Pourquoi ce profil ici :**

- `Engine.free` est un `Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn Backend>>>` : une requête par backend.
- `PREFILL_CHUNK = 256` existe, mais le chunking est par requête, sans ordonnanceur global.
- `Convoy` mutualise des passes, mais ne planifie pas les requêtes.
- Le KV est contigu par séquence, non paginé.
- `MAX_CONNECTIONS = 64`, `Connection: close`, pas de keep-alive.
- C’est le prochain plafond de scalabilité après le préfill : c4/c16/c64, TTFT, p99.

**Livrables 90 jours :**

1. Design doc + prototype d’ordonnanceur token-level.
2. Pool KV N × contexte ; chunked prefill ; annulation ; métriques par token.
3. Benchmarks c4/c16/c64 avec p99 et TTFT.
4. Préservation de l’exactitude et des invariants Warm Start/Convoy.

**KPI :** débit agrégé, p99, TTFT, cache hit, zéro régression d’exactitude.

---

### P0/P1 — 3. Ingénieur quantification et exactitude numérique

**Mission :** étendre la quantification et garantir que chaque gain de vitesse reste exact.

**Compétences indispensables :**

- **GGUF**, quantization par blocs, K-quants, grilles IQ, MXFP4, NVFP4, FP8 E4M3, **imatrix**.
- **Analyse numérique** : référence f64, propagation d’erreur, tolérances, ordre d’accumulation, fp16/bf16/fp8, arrondi stochastique.
- **Encodeur** `quantize`, politique par tenseur, requantification, split/merge.
- **Tests différentiels**, property-based, fuzzing, conformance vs llama.cpp.
- **Sensibilité performance** : dequant-in-registers, vectorisation, layouts compatibles noyaux.

**Pourquoi ce profil ici :**

- 5 cibles de quantification contre ~30 ; pas d’imatrix ni d’IQ encode.
- NVFP4 et F8_E4M3 absents du runtime.
- KV f16 seulement ; q8_0/q4_0 manquants.
- L’exactitude est le différenciateur produit : un gain de vitesse qui change la sortie n’est pas mergeable.
- `kinetic-quant` est déjà la définition de référence ; `kdot/tests.rs` compare chaque noyau. Il faut étendre cette discipline, pas la réinventer.

**Livrables 90 jours :**

1. Runtime NVFP4/FP8.
2. IQ encode + imatrix.
3. KV q8/q4 correct.
4. Corpus de conformance, tests property/fuzz, gates d’identité.
5. Métriques qualité (KL/perplexité) par format.

**KPI :** qualité, vitesse, mémoire, zéro régression d’identité.

---

### P0/P1 — 4. Architecte Rust systèmes / backend

**Mission :** réduire la duplication CUDA/Vulkan et préparer HIP/Metal/SYCL sans multiplier les exécuteurs.

**Compétences indispensables :**

- **Rust avancé** : lifetimes, traits, génériques vs `dyn`, zéro-copie, soundness `unsafe`, `Send`/`Sync`, `Arc`/`Rc`, mmap, allocators, layouts cache-friendly, monomorphisation.
- **Architecture** : ports/adapters, abstraction backend, graphe/dispatch, feature flags, compilation conditionnelle, FFI.
- **Performance hôte** : `perf`, flamegraph, heaptrack, criterion, LLVM optimization remarks, LTO/PGO/BOLT, démarrage.
- **Build** : workspaces Cargo, cross-compilation, toolchains CUDA/HIP, CI.
- **Tests** : unitaires, intégration, property-based, fuzz, tests déterministes.

**Pourquoi ce profil ici :**

- `kinetic-models/src/cuda` ≈ 4,5 k LOC vs `vulkan` ≈ 2,2 k LOC ; `kinetic-cuda` ≈ 8,5 k LOC vs `kinetic-vulkan` ≈ 5,9 k LOC.
- Ajouter HIP va dupliquer encore ; il faut une couche d’exécution/dispatch minimale, pas un compilateur généraliste.
- Les bons seams existent déjà : `Family`, `Target`, `Backend`, `Projector`. Il faut les préserver.
- La surface `unsafe` est concentrée aux frontières SIMD/GPU/FFI ; un audit de soundness est nécessaire.
- Le démarrage et le cache de pipelines sont des gains faciles.

**Livrables 90 jours :**

1. Cartographie de la duplication ; proposition d’une couche partagée minimale.
2. Refactor d’un chemin comme preuve (FFN/attention) sans changer le comportement.
3. Audit `unsafe` avec commentaires `SAFETY`.
4. Amélioration du démarrage et du temps de build.
5. API prête pour 3+ backends.

**KPI :** LOC dupliquées, temps de build, démarrage, overhead hôte par token, nombre d’`unsafe` justifiés.

---

### P0 — 5. Ingénieur performance / qualification

**Mission :** rendre la mesure automatisée, reproductible et infalsifiable.

**Compétences indispensables :**

- **Méthodologie** : médianes, intervalles de confiance, bruit ±5–10 %, A/B avec contrôles avant/après, état thermique et fréquences, isolation.
- **Harness** : Python/Rust, JSON, `ledger.jsonl`, détection de régression, CI GPU, artefacts épinglés.
- **Profilage** : RGP, rocprof, Nsight, `perf`, watchdogs mémoire.
- **Tests** : fuzzing, soak, needle à 50 %/100 % de contexte, conformance, chaos (`server_abuse.py`).
- **Reproductibilité** : révisions de poids, commits moteur, versions de driver, conteneurs.

**Pourquoi ce profil ici :**

- Le protocole existe déjà dans `PLAN.md` et `llama-kinetic.md` §7.10, mais il est manuel.
- Pas de CI GPU : les régressions de noyaux ne sont pas détectées automatiquement.
- Les chiffres sont la crédibilité du projet ; il faut un `THEORY.md`, un ledger et des portes de sortie.
- Les scripts existent (`bench_protocol.py`, `bench_vs_llamacpp.py`, `conformance.py`, `server_abuse.py`, `same_answer_demo.py`) : il faut les industrialiser.

**Livrables 90 jours :**

1. `THEORY.md` avec les plafonds mesurés (bande passante, FLOPS, KV).
2. `ledger.jsonl` + `configs/` + `best-config.json`.
3. A/B automatisé avec contrôles.
4. CI GPU (au moins un runner Vulkan/ROCm) avec seuil de régression.
5. Qualification de release : build propre, poids épinglés, gates.

**KPI :** taux de faux positifs/négatifs, temps de détection d’une régression, couverture des gates.

---

### P1 — 6. Ingénieur intégration des architectures

**Compétences :**

- Zoo Transformer : MHA/GQA/MQA/**MLA**/**DSA**/attention sinks, RoPE/iRoPE/partial/scaling, MoE top-k/shared/sigmoid, SSM/hybride (Mamba2, RWKV, delta net), norm/activation, T5 encodeur-décodeur, têtes embedding/rerank/TTS.
- Lecture GGUF (metadata + tensor map), mapping vers `blocks/`, descripteurs déclaratifs.
- Conformance vs llama.cpp, gates d’identité.
- Discipline : **un fichier par famille**, pas de `match` central.

**Pourquoi :** 21/180 architectures. Les briques les plus rentables sont MLA/DSA, les hybrides SSM et T5. Les modèles locaux bloqués sont `qwen3vl`, `deepseek`, `llama4`, `gemma2`, `phi3`, `command-r`, `dbrx`.

**Livrables :** lots d’architectures par brique réutilisable, tests de conformance, documentation `models.md`.

**KPI :** modèles chargés, tokens identiques à llama.cpp, couverture.

---

### P1 — 7. Ingénieur tokenizers / templates / tool calls

**Compétences :**

- BPE, SentencePiece, WordPiece, **UGM**, **Tekken**, prétokenizers regex, byte-level, tokens spéciaux EOT/EOM/FIM.
- Templates Jinja, formats de tool calls (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, InternLM, Command-R…), JSON Schema/GBNF.
- Tests différentiels vs `llama-tokenize` et `llama-server`.

**Pourquoi :** 13/68 prétokenizers, 55 manquants ; templates intégrés et formats tool-call incomplets ; l’issue #5 (tool calls dans le raisonnement) est typique.

**Livrables :** 15 prétokenizers prioritaires, UGM, split GGUF, templates intégrés, formats tool-call.

**KPI :** ids identiques sur un corpus de contrôle, requêtes serveur compatibles.

---

### P1 — 8. Ingénieur serveur / API / observabilité

**Compétences :**

- HTTP/1.1, SSE, keep-alive, chunked, timeouts, backpressure, TLS, API keys, CORS, arrêt propre.
- APIs OpenAI, llama-server, Anthropic Messages, Ollama ; `n > 1`, `timings_per_token`, `/props`, `/slots`, `/infill`, `/apply-template`, `/lora-adapters`.
- Prometheus, logs structurés, tracing, p99.
- Sécurité : limites d’entrée, DoS, path traversal.

**Pourquoi :** ~15/45 routes, pas de keep-alive/TLS, 64 connexions thread-per-connection, `docker stop` à améliorer, compatibilité clients perfectible.

**Livrables :** routes manquantes, `n > 1`, TLS/API key, router multi-modèle, métriques, arrêt propre.

**KPI :** conformité llama-server, overhead, stabilité sous charge.

---

### P2 — 9. Ingénieur multimodal

**Compétences :** ViT/SigLIP/CLIP, projecteurs (MLP/merger/Q-Former), preprocessing image, vidéo, audio (mel, ASR/TTS), OCR, noyaux GPU vision.

**Pourquoi :** 2/73 projecteurs, pas d’audio/vidéo/OCR. Impact produit fort mais chantier XL, hors chemin critique de performance.

**Livrables :** 10 projecteurs majeurs, crate `kinetic-audio`, pipeline OCR.

**KPI :** parité des embeddings vs `llama-mtmd`, qualité des réponses.

---

### P2 — 10. Ingénieur build/release/bindings

**Compétences :** Cargo, cross-compilation, toolchains CUDA/HIP, Docker, GitHub Actions, signature de code, winget/scoop, maturin/PyO3, ABI C, semver, mdBook.

**Pourquoi :** 10/200 fonctions C, bindings Python partiels, images Docker et packaging à finaliser.

**Livrables :** ABI C complète, bindings générés, images Docker, installateurs, CI release.

**KPI :** couverture ABI, temps/taille de build, taux d’installation réussie.

## 3. Composition d’équipe recommandée

### Cellule « performance » minimale (5 personnes)

| Rôle | Rôle exact | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| GPU AMD | Vulkan d’abord, HIP ensuite | Le seul écart mesuré est le préfill/MoE |
| Runtime | Ordonnanceur, KV, concurrence | Le prochain plafond après le préfill |
| Rust systèmes | Abstraction backend, dette | Évite de dupliquer HIP/Metal/SYCL |
| Numérique | Quantification + gates | Protège le différenciateur exactitude |
| Performance/QA | CI GPU, ledger, A/B | Sans mesure, pas de gain prouvé |

### Équipe complète (9–10 personnes)

Ajouter : **intégration modèles**, **tokenizers/templates**, **serveur/API**, **multimodal**, **build/release/bindings**.

### Séquencement

| Phase | Durée | Rôles | Objectif |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Mesure | 2–4 sem. | QA + GPU | Baseline, `THEORY.md`, CI GPU |
| 1. Préfill | 6–10 sem. | GPU + numérique + QA | GEMM tuilé, coopmat, async, pp ≥ 2× |
| 2. MoE/HIP | 8–12 sem. | GPU + runtime + Rust | MoE groupé, squelette HIP, KV q8 |
| 3. Concurrence | 6–10 sem. | Runtime + Rust + QA | Ordonnanceur, cN, TTFT |
| 4. Couverture | continu | Modèles + tokenizers + serveur | Architectures, prétokenizers, routes |
| 5. Produit | continu | Multimodal + build | Vision/audio, bindings |

### Matrice chantier → pilote

| Chantier | Pilote | Support | Porte de sortie |
|---|---|---|---|
| GEMM préfill Vulkan | GPU AMD | Numérique, QA | pp512 ≥ 2×, bit-exact |
| MoE Vulkan | GPU AMD | Runtime, Numérique | tg/pp, qualité |
| HIP/ROCm | GPU AMD/HIP | Rust architect | vs llama ROCm0 |
| Ordonnanceur/KV | Runtime | Rust, QA | cN, p99, TTFT |
| Quantification | Numérique | GPU/CPU kernel | Identité |
| Architectures | Intégration modèles | Numérique, QA | Conformance |
| Tokenizers | Tokenizers | Serveur | Ids identiques |
| API serveur | Serveur | QA | Conformance |
| CI perf | QA | Build/release | Régression |
| Bindings | Build/release | Serveur | Tests ABI |

## 4. Comment évaluer ces experts

Éviter les entretiens théoriques. Donner un **exercice tiré du dépôt**, avec mesure et gate d’exactitude.

| Rôle | Exercice |
|---|---|
| GPU AMD | Implémenter un GEMM tuilé Q4_K dans `gemv_many.wgsl` ou un nouveau shader ; le profiler avec RGP ; battre l’existant de ≥ 1,5× ; passer le test bit-exact. |
| Runtime | Concevoir un ordonnanceur continuous batching pour `Engine`/`Sequence` ; expliquer le rollback KV, l’annulation, la fairness ; identifier les impacts sur RAD-1/Warm Start. |
| Rust systèmes | Refactoriser un chemin dupliqué CUDA/Vulkan derrière une abstraction minimale, sans changer les tests ; expliquer `Send`/`Sync` et les `unsafe`. |
| Numérique | Implémenter un format de bloc de la référence f64 au noyau, avec tests différentiels et mesure. |
| Intégration modèles | Ajouter une famille à partir d’un GGUF inconnu, en un fichier + une ligne, et la comparer à llama.cpp. |
| Tokenizers | Faire passer un corpus de contrôle avec les mêmes ids que `llama-tokenize`, tokens spéciaux compris. |
| QA | Concevoir un A/B qui détecte une régression de 5 % avec un bruit de ±8 % ; calculer la taille d’échantillon et les contrôles. |

**Signaux d’alerte :**

- Uniquement PyTorch/TensorFlow, aucune notion de noyau ou de mémoire.
- CUDA uniquement, incapable de lire du WGSL/SPIR-V ou de raisonner RDNA.
- « Il suffit de réécrire en X » sans mesure ni migration incrémentale.
- Benchmarks sans contrôles, sans médiane, sans état machine.
- Aucune sensibilité à l’exactitude : « on verra plus tard ».
- Impossible de lire un profil GPU ou d’expliquer memory-bound vs compute-bound.

---

## 5. Ce qu’il ne faut pas faire

- **Ne pas recruter un « expert LLM » générique en premier.** Le goulot est GPU/runtime, pas la théorie des transformers.
- **Ne pas commencer par HIP.** Le décodage Vulkan est déjà à 95 % ; le préfill est à 23 %. Le GEMM Vulkan est le meilleur premier chantier.
- **Ne pas recruter un expert CUDA-only pour ce fork.** La machine n’a pas de GPU NVIDIA ; il ne pourrait rien mesurer. CUDA est utile en amont/CI, pas en P0 local.
- **Ne pas lancer un chantier multimodal ou bindings avant la performance.** C’est XL et hors chemin critique.
- **Ne pas introduire un compilateur de graphes généraliste.** Une couche de dispatch/exécution minimale suffit ; le projet n’a pas besoin de MLIR.
- **Ne pas casser la culture d’exactitude.** Un gain non prouvé, ou qui change la sortie, doit être rejeté.

---

## 6. Recommandation finale

Si je devais n’embaucher que **quatre personnes** pour ce dépôt :

1. **Ingénieur noyaux GPU AMD** — le plus gros gain mesuré, le plus rare.
2. **Architecte runtime d’inférence** — le prochain plafond de scalabilité.
3. **Ingénieur performance/qualification** — pour que les deux premiers prouvent leurs gains.
4. **Ingénieur quantification/exactitude** — pour que ces gains restent conformes à la promesse produit.

Si un seul profil : **GPU AMD avec une forte sensibilité quantification/exactitude**. C’est le seul qui attaque directement l’écart de 4,4× en préfill et de 3,3–5,4× en MoE.

Si deux : ajouter **runtime**. Si trois : ajouter **QA/perf**. Si quatre : ajouter **numérique**.

Le reste — architectures, tokenizers, serveur, multimodal, bindings — peut être parallélisé, communautarisé ou recruté ensuite. Le projet a déjà les bons seams (`Family`, `Target`, `Backend`, `Projector`) et une documentation d’onboarding solide (`adding-a-family.md`, `contributing.md`) : un bon expert doit pouvoir livrer une famille ou un noyau en quelques jours, pas en quelques semaines.

### Architecture correction

We need to articulate the target:

**Principe** : un seul backend complet par API graphique.
- `kinetic-cuda` : tout CUDA — driver, kernels, layouts, executor, graphes, mémoire, capabilities.
- `kinetic-vulkan` : tout Vulkan — driver, kernels WGSL/SPIR-V, executor, graphes, mémoire, capabilities.
- `kinetic-cpu` : tout CPU — kernels SIMD, thread pool, executor.
- `kinetic-models` : aucune dépendance à CUDA/Vulkan ; décrit les architectures, blocs, tenseurs, spéculatif, warm start, shortlist, convoy ; appelle une interface backend.
- `kinetic-runtime` (nouveau, optionnel) : traits `Backend`, `Device`, `Graph`, `Kernel`, `Capabilities`, `Memory` ; planification générique ; pas de code spécifique à une API.
- `kinetic-hip`, `kinetic-metal`, `kinetic-sycl`, `kinetic-webgpu` : backends de compatibilité, chacun complet pour son API, ajoutés seulement quand une cible le justifie. L'utilisateur charge un seul backend à l'exécution selon sa carte.

**Règle** : pas de module `kinetic-models/src/cuda` ni `kinetic-models/src/vulkan` à terme. Le code d'exécution vit dans le crate backend. `kinetic-models` ne contient que la sémantique du modèle et les invariants d'exactitude.

**Chemin de migration incrémental** :
1. Introduire `kinetic-runtime` avec les traits et les types de capabilities (pas de réécriture).
2. Déplacer `kinetic-models/src/cuda` vers `kinetic-cuda/src/executor` (ou `model`), en gardant les tests.
3. Déplacer `kinetic-models/src/vulkan` vers `kinetic-vulkan/src/executor`.
4. Faire de `kinetic-models` un crate sans features `cuda`/`vulkan` ; il dépend de `kinetic-runtime` uniquement.
5. Adapter `kinetic-server` pour choisir un backend via une factory (`BackendKind::Cuda`, `Vulkan`, `Cpu`) et ne charger que celui-là.
6. Ajouter HIP/Metal/SYCL derrière le même trait, sans toucher `kinetic-models`.

**Bénéfices** :
- Une seule implémentation par API : pas de divergence entre `kinetic-models/src/cuda` et `kinetic-cuda`.
- Les fonctionnalités CUDA (flash attention, MoE, graphs, layer split) vivent dans `kinetic-cuda`, pas éparpillées.
- Les fonctionnalités Vulkan (WGSL, coopmat, async) vivent dans `kinetic-vulkan`.
- `kinetic-models` reste testable sans GPU, avec un backend de test.
- Ajouter un backend = un crate + une factory, pas une modification du cœur.

**Contrainte** : ne pas casser les performances. Le déplacement doit être mécanique d'abord, puis les optimisations. Les tests d'identité doivent rester verts à chaque étape.

**Note sur "les autres backends"** : HIP/Metal/SYCL sont des cibles de compatibilité. On fournit le socle (trait, capabilities, tests de conformance, modèle de build), pas une implémentation complète tant qu'il n'y a pas de machine/CI pour la valider. C'est exactement la règle du `PLAN.md` : pas de travail invérifiable.

1: # Benchmarks
2: 
3: Speed claims are only useful if you can check them on your own machine. This
4: page describes how Kinetic is measured against llama.cpp, how to repeat it,
5: and the results on our reference machines.
6: 
7: ## Method
8: 
9: - **Same file, same threads.** Both engines run the same GGUF file. On the
10:   CPU both get the same thread count; on the GPU both run the whole model on
11:   the device.
12: - **The llama-bench tests.** `pp512` processes a 512-token prompt and
13:   `tg128` generates 128 tokens. `kinetic bench` runs the same two tests as
14:   `llama-bench`, with speculative decoding off, so every generated token
15:   costs one pass over the weights on both sides. Each number is the best of
16:   the repetitions.
17: - **An editing request.** Real use often repeats text: an assistant
18:   rewriting code, quoting a document, filling a template. The edit test sends
19:   one greedy chat request that renames a variable in a short Python file and
20:   asks for the whole file back, to `kinetic serve` and to `llama-server` with
21:   llama.cpp's own speculative decoding on (`--spec-type ngram-mod`, or
22:   `draft-mtp` for models with a prediction block). Speed is generated tokens
23:   over the time from the first to the last token, measured on the client the
24:   same way for both. Both answers are greedy, so they should be identical;
25:   the script reports whether they are.
26: - **Exactness is checked, not assumed.** `kinetic bench` also runs its own
27:   edit test and fails if drafted output differs from plain decoding.
28: - **A quiet machine.** No other programs using the CPU or the GPU, laptops
29:   on mains power with the performance power plan, best of three runs.
30: 
31: ## Reproduce it
32: 
33: You need a llama.cpp build with `llama-bench` and `llama-server` and a
34: model file. On the CPU, one script runs everything and prints a markdown
35: table:
36: 
37: ```sh
38: python scripts/bench_vs_llamacpp.py model.gguf --llama-dir path/to/llama.cpp/bin -t 6
39: ```
40: 
41: | Option | Meaning |
42: |---|---|
43: | `--llama-dir` | folder with `llama-bench` and `llama-server` |
44: | `--kinetic` | the `kinetic` binary [default: `kinetic` on `PATH`] |
45: | `-t`, `--threads` | CPU threads for both [default: half the logical CPUs] |
46: | `-r`, `--repetitions` | runs of each plain test [default: 3] |
47: | `--max-tokens` | limit for the edit answer [default: 512] |
48: | `--llama-spec` | `llama-server --spec-type` [default: `ngram-mod`]; use `draft-mtp` for models with an MTP block |
49: | `--skip-edit` | only the two plain tests |
50: 
51: The script hides the GPUs from llama.cpp and passes `--device cpu` to
52: Kinetic, starts one server at a time on 127.0.0.1 and stops it afterwards.
53: 
54: On the GPU, run the two tools by hand:
55: 
56: ```sh
57: kinetic bench model.gguf --device cuda -r 3
58: llama-bench -m model.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -r 3 -ngl 99 -fa on
59: ```
60:

# Building from source

Kinetic is a Cargo workspace of small crates. Building it needs only Rust;
the CUDA kernels also need the CUDA toolkit.

## Requirements

- **Rust 1.91 or newer.** Install it with [rustup](https://rustup.rs).
- **Windows:** the MSVC build tools (Visual Studio 2022 or its Build Tools,
  with "Desktop development with C++").
- **Linux:** a C toolchain (`build-essential` on Debian and Ubuntu).
- **For NVIDIA GPUs:** the [CUDA toolkit](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads)
  12.8 or newer, for `nvcc`. It is needed only at build time: the binary opens
  the driver at runtime and links no CUDA library.

## Build

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Veloresearch/kinetic
cd kinetic
cargo build --release -p kinetic-cli
target/release/kinetic --version
```

The `cuda` feature is on by default. The build looks for `nvcc` in `$NVCC`,
then in `$CUDA_PATH/bin`, then on `PATH`. Without it the build still
succeeds and prints `warning: nvcc not found: CUDA kernels not built`; that
binary runs on the CPU and says so when you ask for `--device cuda`. To build
without CUDA at all:

```sh
cargo build --release -p kinetic-cli --no-default-features
```

On Windows, `nvcc` needs `cl.exe`. From a plain shell, the build finds the
newest MSVC toolset through `vswhere` and passes it to `nvcc`, so a developer
prompt is not required.

The kernels are compiled for every NVIDIA architecture from Pascal (sm_60) to
Blackwell (sm_120), plus PTX that newer drivers can compile for later GPUs.
`KINETIC_CUDA_ARCHS` builds for chosen compute capabilities only, which is
much faster, with PTX for the last of them:

```sh
KINETIC_CUDA_ARCHS="60;61" cargo build --release -p kinetic-cli --features cuda
```

Pascal and Volta (sm_60 to sm_70) need CUDA 12: CUDA 13 no longer builds
for them, so with CUDA 13 the build leaves them out and says so in a
warning, and a binary built that way reports on those GPUs that it has no
kernels for them.

Install the binary into `~/.cargo/bin`:

```sh
cargo install --path crates/kinetic-cli
```

## The libraries

```sh
cargo build --release -p kinetic-capi        # kinetic_capi.dll / libkinetic_capi.so
```

The Python package lives outside the workspace, so that building the engine
never needs Python, and builds with [maturin](https://www.maturin.rs):

```sh
cd bindings/python
pip install "maturin>=1.5,<2"
maturin build --release
pip install target/wheels/kinetic_engine-*.whl
```

## Docker

```sh
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t kinetic .              # CPU
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.cuda -t kinetic:cuda .    # NVIDIA GPUs
```

Both images run `kinetic serve` on port 8080 as an unprivileged user; see
[Install](install.md#docker).

## Tests

```sh
cargo test --release --workspace
```

Tests that need a real model are marked `#[ignore]`. Point them at a file
with `KINETIC_TEST_GGUF` and include them:

```sh
KINETIC_TEST_GGUF=SmolLM2-135M-Instruct-f16.gguf \
  cargo test --release -p kinetic-models --test architectures -- --ignored
```

The CUDA kernel tests run when a GPU and the kernels are present and print
`skipped: ...` otherwise; the model tests on the GPU take `--features cuda`
on `kinetic-models`. Test in release mode: real models in a debug build are
very slow.

## Checks before a pull request

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --release --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test --release --workspace
```

CI runs the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, builds the C example with
`gcc`, `clang` and `cl`, and builds and tests the Python package.

### Architecture section details

Let's write the target architecture precisely.

**Current state:**

| Couche | CUDA | Vulkan | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Driver/kernels | `kinetic-cuda` (8.5k) | `kinetic-vulkan` (5.9k) | `kinetic-cpu` (6.4k) |
| Exécution modèle | `kinetic-models/src/cuda` (4.5k) | `kinetic-models/src/vulkan` (2.2k) | `kinetic-models/src/model.rs` + `kinetic-server/src/cpu.rs` |
| Modèle/arch | `kinetic-models/src/arch`, `blocks` | same | same |
| Serveur | `kinetic-server/src/cuda.rs` | `kinetic-server/src/vulkan.rs` | `kinetic-server/src/cpu.rs` |

**Problem**: CUDA functionality is split between `kinetic-cuda` and `kinetic-models/src/cuda`; Vulkan between `kinetic-vulkan` and `kinetic-models/src/vulkan`. This is not "one backend per API"; it's two layers per API, and the model crate has backend-specific features. Adding HIP would create `kinetic-hip` + `kinetic-models/src/hip`.

**Target:**

```
kinetic-models        (arch, blocks, speculative, warm, shortlist, convoy; no backend feature)
        │
kinetic-runtime       (traits: Backend, Device, Graph, Kernel, Capabilities, Memory; scheduler-agnostic)
        │
├── kinetic-cpu       (all CPU: SIMD kernels, thread pool, executor)
├── kinetic-cuda      (all CUDA: driver, kernels, layouts, executor, graphs, layer split, MoE)
├── kinetic-vulkan    (all Vulkan: loader, WGSL/SPIR-V, executor, graphs, coopmat, async)
└── kinetic-hip       (compatibility, all HIP, added when a machine/CI can validate it)
```

**Rules:**
- `kinetic-models` has no `cfg(feature = "cuda"|"vulkan")`, no `cuda/` or `vulkan/` modules. It describes the model and the semantics; it calls the runtime traits.
- Each backend crate owns everything for its API: device discovery, memory, kernels, graph capture, executor, capability declaration, error mapping.
- `kinetic-server` selects exactly one backend at runtime (`auto|cpu|cuda|vulkan|hip`) and does not link the others' code paths into the hot path. Features can still compile them in, but the runtime uses one.
- Compatibility backends (HIP, Metal, SYCL, WebGPU) implement the same trait; they are added only when there is a machine/CI to validate them, per `PLAN.md`.
- The `Backend` trait must be rich enough to express: device capabilities, supported weight types, graph capture, async submission, memory placement (layer/expert/tensor), KV cache, sampling on device, and error handling. It must not leak CUDA/Vulkan types.
- Keep `Target` (speculative) and `Family` (architectures) as they are; they are good seams.

**Migration steps:**
1. Create `kinetic-runtime` with traits and capability types; no behavior change.
2. Move `kinetic-models/src/cuda` into `kinetic-cuda/src/executor` (mechanical move, keep tests).
3. Move `kinetic-models/src/vulkan` into `kinetic-vulkan/src/executor`.
4. Remove `cuda`/`vulkan` features from `kinetic-models`; `kinetic-models` depends only on `kinetic-runtime`.
5. Add a `BackendFactory` in `kinetic-server`/`kinetic-cli` that picks one backend; remove backend-specific branches from the engine.
6. Add a `TestBackend` (CPU or mock) to test `kinetic-models` without GPU.
7. Only then optimize: the refactor is mechanical first; perf work after.
8. Add HIP/Metal/SYCL as separate crates implementing `kinetic-runtime`; no changes to `kinetic-models`.

**Non-goals:**
- No full graph compiler / MLIR.
- No dynamic plugin ABI at first; compile-time features are fine.
- No backend-specific code in `kinetic-models`.
- No "universal kernel" that is slower on all backends; each backend optimizes its own path.

**Why this matters for experts:**
- The Rust/backend architect owns this migration.
- The GPU AMD expert works inside `kinetic-vulkan` and `kinetic-hip`, not in `kinetic-models`.
- The runtime architect works in `kinetic-runtime` and `kinetic-server`, not in backend crates.
- The quantization expert works in `kinetic-quant` and the kernel crates, with a shared reference.
- The model integration expert works only in `kinetic-models/src/arch` and `blocks`, with no backend code.

This is a clean separation of responsibilities.

--- scripts/llama_presets.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check that every path a llama.cpp router preset names exists.

Reads `presets.ini` (the file `llama-server --models-preset` takes), and
reports the `model`, `mmproj`, `lora` and `chat-template-file` paths that are
missing, which are exactly the presets the router cannot load.

With `--write`, also appends a section for each GGUF model folder under
`--models` that no existing section already names, so a model added to the
kinetic folder shows up in the router without hand-editing the file. Existing
sections, and their tuned options, are never rewritten.

    python scripts/llama_presets.py
    python scripts/llama_presets.py --write
"""

import argparse
import configparser
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PATHS = ("model", "mmproj", "lora", "chat-template-file")


def sections(path):
    parser = configparser.ConfigParser()
    parser.optionxform = str
    parser.read(path)
    return parser


def check(path):
    parser = sections(path)
    missing = 0
    for section in parser.sections():
        if section == "*":
            continue
        for key in PATHS:
            value = parser[section].get(key)
            if value and not Path(value).exists():
                print(f"{section}: {key} is missing: {value}")
                missing += 1
    return missing

"""Starts a new model family from a GGUF file.

Prints the file's architecture, its `<arch>.*` metadata and the tensors of
one layer, writes crates/kinetic-models/src/arch/<name>.rs as a Llama-style
starter that builds, and adds it to the family list. What is left is
mapping the tensors onto blocks; see docs/src/adding-a-family.md.

    python scripts/new_family.py model.gguf
    python scripts/new_family.py model.gguf --dry-run

Standard library only; reads the header, never the weights.
"""

import argparse
import os
import re
import struct
import sys

ARCH_DIR = os.path.join("crates", "kinetic-models", "src", "arch")

# GGUF value types, see the GGUF spec in ggml's docs/gguf.md
SCALARS = {0: "<B", 1: "<b", 2: "<H", 3: "<h", 4: "<I", 5: "<i", 6: "<f", 7: "<?",
           10: "<Q", 11: "<q", 12: "<d"}
STRING, ARRAY = 8, 9


class Reader:
    def __init__(self, f):
        self.f = f

    def unpack(self, fmt):
        return struct.unpack(fmt, self.f.read(struct.calcsize(fmt)))[0]

    def string(self):
        return self.f.read(self.unpack("<Q")).decode("utf-8", "replace")

    def value(self, ty):
        if ty == STRING:
            return self.string()
        if ty == ARRAY:
            inner, n = self.unpack("<I"), self.unpack("<Q")
            items = [self.value(inner) for _ in range(n)]
            return items if n <= 64 else f"[{n} items]"
